The Atlas of Regenerative Materials

The Atlas of Regenerative Materials is collecting knowledge and know-how on availability and use of regenerative materials for construction. Data is structured in 5 entities: Resource, Buidling Material, Construction Technique, Professionals and Buildings. Taxonomies for all entities and for buiding elements help filter the dataset. 

Every entry consists at least of: 
- Title
- Descriptive Text
- Material Tag (Earth, Straw, Hemp, Wood, Stone, Other Fibres, Re-Used)
- One multimedia item
- Entry author

Where applicable, adress(es), relations to other entries or to taxonomy items, external links and other entity-specific details can be added, as well as further textual information.

Data on Zenodo

Here on this repository we share and store snapshots every 12 months. The dataset consists of tables for each entity of the Atlas of Regenerative Materials and the authors as well as the taxonomies. Additionnally GIS data on resource potentials is available for Switzerland and parts of Europe as far as they are being produced.

Data structure from snapshots

  • Entities: Here are all textual inputs and relations from the entries, grouped by entity
  • Files: Here lie all multimedia documents related to the entries
  • Taxonomies: All taxonomies used for characterisation of the entries

metadata.title: CleanCloud CHOPIN - multi-frequency radar data
metadata.description:
This repository contains the code & data referenced in the ESSD manuscript "Multi-frequency radar measurements of clouds and precipitation collected during the 2024-2025 CHOPIN campaign at Mt. Helmos".

 

Manuscript abstract:

This article describes the dataset of cloud and precipitation measurements collected during the CleanCloud Helmos OrograPhic sIte experimeNt (CHOPIN) campaign, conducted from October 2024 to January 2025 on Mt. Helmos, Peloponnese, Greece. The data were collected by the Environmental Remote Sensing Laboratory of the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL) and comprise coordinated observations from X- and Ka-band dual-polarisation Doppler radars and a W-band Doppler cloud profiler, complemented by 37 radiosonde profiles. Precipitation occurred for approximately 440 hours, resulting in roughly 1.2 m of snow accumulation at the remote sensing site. Two precipitation events are presented to illustrate the two main cloud and precipitation regimes captured in the dataset. The first event, between 6 and 8 January 2025, captures a succession of shallow turbulent orographic clouds interspersed with higher non-precipitating clouds, with a brief episode of surface-reaching precipitation from the upper cloud layer. The second case study, on 15 January 2025, shows a mixed-phase precipitation system dominated by primary ice nucleation near cloud top, particle growth through deposition and aggregation, and signatures of riming in the lower cloud layers, within a dynamically evolving synoptic context. Together, these examples highlight the potential of multi-frequency radar observations in an orographic winter setting for investigating cloud microphysics, particle growth processes, and aerosol--cloud interactions in mixed-phase clouds. As a dataset combining wintertime orographic conditions with coordinated multi-frequency radar observations, and collected alongside an extensive suite of in situ cloud microphysical and aerosol measurements within the broader CleanCloud campaign, the CHOPIN radar data opens new possibilities for mixed-phase cloud microphysics and aerosol-cloud interaction studies.

 

Note that L1 radar data (in netCDF format) is available on the ACTRIS Cloudnet data portal, instruments "LAPI MXPol weather radar", "LATMOS BASTA Doppler non-scanning cloud radar" and "METEK MIRA-35S (MBR5) Doppler scanning cloud radar" (more details can be found in the manuscript).

metadata.title: Geo-trax: A Comprehensive Framework for Georeferenced Vehicle Trajectory Extraction from Drone Imagery
metadata.description:
Geo-trax (GEO-referenced TRAjectory eXtraction) is a comprehensive pipeline that extracts high-accuracy, georeferenced vehicle trajectories from high-altitude drone imagery. Built for quasi-stationary aerial monitoring of urban traffic, it turns raw bird's-eye view (BEV) drone footage into precise, real-world vehicle trajectories. The framework combines YOLO detection, multi-object tracking, and video stabilization with a robust orthophoto-based georeferencing stage, producing geo-coordinated, lane-resolved trajectories that are spatially and temporally consistent and ready for large-scale traffic analysis and simulation. It is optimized for urban intersections and arterial corridors, where high-fidelity, vehicle-level insights drive intelligent transportation systems and digital twin applications.

📌 Important: If you use this code in your work, kindly acknowledge it by citing the following article:

Robert Fonod, Haechan Cho, Hwasoo Yeo, Nikolas Geroliminis (2025). Advanced computer vision for extracting georeferenced vehicle trajectories from drone imagery, Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies, vol. 178, 105205. DOI: 10.1016/j.trc.2025.105205

📖 Documentation: rfonod.github.io/geo-trax, with a guide per pipeline stage, setup guides for configuration and your own data, and a CLI and configuration reference generated from the code.

Why Geo-trax

  • 🛰️ Real-world output: georeferenced, lane-resolved trajectories (WGS84 + local CRS) with per-vehicle speed, acceleration, and estimated dimensions, straight from raw BEV drone video.
  • 🎯 Accurate detection: YOLOv8s vehicle detector reaching 0.951 mAP@50, trained on more than 19,000 annotated aerial images.
  • 🚗 Flexible tracking: four vehicle classes and six selectable multi-object trackers (BoT-SORT, ByteTrack, OC-SORT, and more).
  • ⚖️ Drone-motion robust: homography-based stabilization (Stabilo) plus orthophoto image registration for consistent, cross-flight coordinates; both optionally CUDA-accelerated.
  • 📊 Proven at scale: powered the Songdo Traffic dataset (roughly 700,000 trajectories across 20 intersections, fleet of 10 drones; see Real-World Deployment below).
  • ⚙️ One command, one config: geotrax batch runs the whole pipeline; a single YAML drives every stage, with four tuned presets included.

Features

  • Detection: YOLOv8s on aerial BEV imagery; detects car (incl. vans), bus, truck, and motorcycle; optional per-class confidence thresholds (extraction.class_conf) and SAHI sliced inference for improved small-object recall (--sahi).
  • Tracking: six multi-object trackers (BoT-SORT default; see Tracking); optional per-track frame-gap interpolation.
  • Stabilization: homography-based trajectory correction via Stabilo ⚖️, tuned with Stabilo-Optimize 🎯; optional CUDA acceleration (--stab-gpu).
  • Georeferencing: frame-to-orthophoto registration; outputs lat/lon, local CRS, speed, acceleration, and lane assignment per vehicle; optional CUDA acceleration (--geo-gpu).
  • Visualization: track overlays on original, stabilized, or static-reference video, in five rendering modes (incl. oriented bounding boxes).
  • Analysis: trajectory maps, kinematic distributions, and class/dimension charts, per-video or aggregated across drones and sessions; GIS export (GeoPackage/GeoJSON) of trajectories for QGIS, ArcGIS, or kepler.gl (geotrax export).
  • Scaling & tooling: batch-processes directory trees and aggregates multi-drone data; includes standalone utilities for end-to-end data preparation, training, evaluation, and validation.

🚀 Planned Enhancements

  • Modularized, OOP-based pipeline with custom reference frame support and georeferencing leveraging Stabilo's image-matching backend.
  • Simulation and scenario export: geotrax export --format sumo (and/or OpenDRIVE, CommonRoad) to turn an extracted dataset into a drop-in scenario for traffic simulators and digital twins, reusing the lane and road-section geometry already carried by the orthophoto segmentations.
  • Live/online mode: ingest RTMP-style drone feeds for real-time georeferenced output, for live monitoring and incident detection rather than offline batches.
  • Batch inference and multi-thread processing, plus distributed fan-out (Ray, Dask, or Slurm) so geotrax batch scales across a cluster for multi-drone, multi-intersection campaigns.
  • Real-world map visualization (e.g., MovingPandas, contextily) and an interactive web viewer with map-based playback and filtering by class, lane, speed, and time, so datasets can be explored without writing plotting code. (geotrax export already produces GeoPackage/GeoJSON layers that open directly in QGIS or kepler.gl.)

🔗 Related Projects

Geo-trax integrates with and complements several specialized tools:

  • Stabilo ⚖️: Python library for video and trajectory stabilization using robust homography transformations. Supports various feature detectors, RANSAC algorithms, and user-defined masks. Used as Geo-trax's core stabilization engine.
  • Stabilo-Optimize 🎯: benchmarking and hyperparameter optimization framework for Stabilo. Evaluates stabilization performance through ground truth-free assessment using random perturbations. Used to fine-tune Geo-trax stabilization parameters.
  • HBB2OBB 📦: converts horizontal bounding boxes to oriented bounding boxes using SAM segmentation models. Can enhance Geo-trax outputs when object orientation is needed for downstream analysis.

Real-World Deployment: The Songdo Experiment

Geo-trax was validated in a large-scale urban traffic monitoring campaign in Songdo, South Korea, where it processed footage from a fleet of 10 drones to produce the Songdo Traffic dataset. The detection model was trained on the companion Songdo Vision dataset. Both are described in the associated publication.

Songdo campaign
📍 LocationSongdo International Business District, South Korea
📅 Duration4 days (October 4 to 7, 2022)
🚁 Fleet10 drones (DJI Mavic 3), 140 to 150 m altitude, 4K at 29.97 fps
🔭 Coverage20 busy intersections
🚗 Result~700,000 georeferenced vehicle trajectories

🎥 Demo of Geo-trax applied to the Songdo experiment: https://youtu.be/gOGivL9FFLk

Citation

If you use Geo-trax in your research or software, please cite:

  1. Journal article (preferred for any use of the framework):

  title = {Advanced computer vision for extracting georeferenced vehicle trajectories from drone imagery},

dc.description.abstract.value:
ArmEpiC: Methodology and Data Description 

ArmEpiC, Armenian Epigraphic Corpus (ArtsakhEpiC Sub-Corpus), is a digital scholarly edition of ten Armenian lapidary inscriptions from Artsakh, diplomatically transcribed and encoded in TEI/EpiDoc (v9.7), together with the controlled-vocabulary authority files needed to interpret them. ArtsakhEpiC is the Artsakh regional sub-corpus of the wider ArmEpiC (Armenian Epigraphic Corpus) initiative, hosted by the EPFL Digital Humanities Laboratory (DHLAB).

Scope of the dataset. The deposit includes ten TEI/EpiDoc inscription files (ART0001–ART0010), each a standalone document with diplomatic transcription, translations in Armenian and English, physical description, dating, and bibliography; twelve authority files covering places and toponyms (ListPlace), monuments and monument parts (ListMonument), preservation and condition states (ListPreservation, cross-referenced to the EAGLE preservation-state vocabulary and Getty AAT), materials (ListMaterial), scripts and hands (ListScript), techniques (ListTechniques), object types (ListObjectType), inscription functional types (ListInscriptionType), abbreviation types (ListAbbreviationType), chronology and dating methods (ListChronology), bibliography (ListBibl), and editors and contributors (ListEditors); ten photographic figures (Fig. 1–Fig. 10, one per inscription); a README; and a licensing statement.

Standards and encoding. All XML files are TEI/EpiDoc 9.7, associated via <?xml-model?> processing instructions with the schema at https://epidoc.stoa.org/schema/9.7/tei-epidoc.rng (both RelaxNG structure and embedded Schematron rules). Authority files are aligned with CIDOC CRM and, where applicable, cross-referenced to EAGLE and the Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus. Each authority entity carries a persistent URN of the form urn:armepic:<vocabulary>:<ID>, and every inscription's editorial responsibility statement references the corresponding editor URN in ListEditors.

Editors and contributors. Hamest Tamrazyan (EPFL DHLAB) — editor-in-chief: project direction, template development, EpiDoc adaptation, terminology and SKOS modelling, authority-file creation. Gayane Hovhannisyan (European University of Armenia) — editor: translation of texts and terminology, EpiDoc adaptation, validation of terminology and SKOS concepts. Arsen Harutyunyan (Institute of Archaeology and Ethnography, NAS RA) — editor: epigraphic research and provision of inscriptional data, EpiDoc adaptation, photographic data collection. Emanuela Boros (EPFL DHLAB) — data curator: technical implementation support, data curation, project co-supervision. Emile Cornamusaz (EPFL) — contributor: technical implementation and automation.

Licensing and versioning. The dataset is released under a Creative Commons Attribution–NonCommercial 4.0 International (CC BY-NC 4.0) license; reuse for research and teaching is welcome with attribution, and commercial use requires the editors' permission. This Zenodo deposit represents a fixed release; future revisions will receive new versions under the same concept DOI.

Funding. This project has been funded by the National Association for Armenian Studies and Research (NAASR), the Knights of Vartan Fund for Armenian Studies, and the Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF, grants IZSEZ0_212008 and IZSEZ0_216747).

What changed in this version. This release corrects a broad set of issues found in the previously published deposit: four inscription files that were not well-formed XML; the editor authority file, rebuilt as a valid, schema-associated TEI document with persistent URNs matching those already referenced by the inscriptions; a license inconsistency across files, now unified to CC BY-NC 4.0 throughout; a missing ListPreservation authority file, now added, resolving preservation-state references used by six of the ten inscriptions; a dead schema URL in all ten inscription files, repointed to the working one already used by the authority files; and filename/asset naming inconsistencies. All 22 XML files were additionally validated against the live EpiDoc 9.7 RelaxNG schema, surfacing and fixing further schema violations across the inscription files (invalid <license> spelling, duplicate single-occurrence elements, misplaced header elements, an invalid content-model mixture in the source description, out-of-order manuscript-identifier elements, and a misplaced pointing attribute) and one authority file (a header ordering error). One inscription record, ART0009, additionally had its title and inscription-type classification corrected: it had been copy-pasted from another record and mislabeled the wrong monument (Gandzasar instead of Dadivank).

Citation. Tamrazyan, H., Hovhannisyan, G., Harutyunyan, A., & Boros, E. ArmEpiC – Armenian Epigraphic Corpus (ArtsakhEpiC Sub-Corpus). Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18198117

dc.description.abstract.value:
General information



Author info: Jules GRANDVILLEMIN, PhD Candidate, EPFL (https://orcid.org/0009-0009-4663-6120).

Date of collection: 19 December, 2025.


 

Description



This dataset provides all the data needed to reproduce the results of a submitted article that evaluates the potential (i.e. possibilities) to practice sustainable mobility in a given area.

To do this, the author calculated three scores, the formulas and data used for each of which are listed in the 'Methodological info' section in the README.txt file:


(i) a score for accessibility to essential daily human needs on foot or by public transport (PT);

(ii) a score for individual motility, i.e. their ability to use PT;

(iii) a synthetic score combining the two previous scores: i.e. accessibility and mobility.

Used the centre of 1580 x 1km² cells (where individuals' residences are located) as the origin of the travels to calculate the accessibility score, so their residence's localisation is not needed;

dc.description.abstract.value:
This directory contains open-source data obtained at the UNFoLD laboratory and BioRob laboratory at EPFL. The data were recorded using the bio-inspired undulatory robot 1-guilla, swimming freely in a pool and tethered in a water channel at various depths. #### Related article The methods and results are described in the paper: *Anastasiadis. A, Ijspeert. A. J., & Mulleners, K. (2026). Tethering and depth of submergence affect the swimming performance of undulatory robots, 2026. arXiv preprint arXiv:2605.03850.* Related article abstract:
Over the past few decades, biomimetic robotic experiments have significantly advanced our understanding of undulatory swimming. Compared to animal experiments, robotic experiments offer repeatability and controlled parameter variations, but the robots operate under constraints that differ from those experienced by their natural counterparts. Freely swimming robots often remain on the surface, whereas most undulatory fish, including eels, are typically fully submerged during locomotion. Studies focusing on submerged swimming commonly rely on tethered robots to maintain depth control. This study examines the performance implications for free versus tethered swimming at the surface, and for tethered swimming at the surface to tethered fully submerged swimming, using the robotic undulatory swimmer 1-guilla. The robot was tested in two configurations: free swimming in a pool and tethered swimming in a water channel at the surface and at varying depths down to three body heights. We varied kinematic input parameters and quantified performance in terms of swimming speed, cost of transport, and body kinematics. Our results reveal that at the surface, tethered swimming achieves speeds comparable to free swimming but at a lower energetic cost. This reduction in cost of transport is attributed to the mechanical stabilisation imposed by tethering, including the suppression of body roll and lateral head motion. Increasing submergence depth improved both the maximum speed and energy efficiency by more than 10% relative to the surface swimming performance. As the body kinematics remained unchanged when submerged, the performance deficit near the surface is attributed to increased wave drag. Overall, our findings provide explanations and insights into discrepancies in results obtained for tethered and free-swimming robotic studies, they highlight the hydrodynamic challenges of surface locomotion, and can help explain why natural undulatory swimmers predominantly favour submerged propulsion.
#### Structure overview This data repository contains the following files: \- `resultsFree.csv` - Experimental parameters and calculated results for experiments with the free swimming version of 1-guilla in the pool. \- `resultsTeth.csv` - Experimental parameters and calculated results for experiments with the tethered swimming version of 1-guilla in the water channel. \- `kinematicsFree/kinematics_msXXXmptYYY_free.csv` - containing individual recorded kinematics for the free-swimming version of the robot in the pool. \- `kinematicsTeth/kinematics_msXXXmptYYY_teth.csv` - containing individual recorded kinematics for the tethered swimming version of the robot in the water. channel \- `load_data.m` - Initial support for loading and visualisation of the data is provided in this file  The data structure and variable descriptions are included in the `readme.md`.

### Supplementary Data — Trained Model Checkpoints and Benchmark Results

This archive set accompanies an anonymous manuscript submission. It contains the final trained model weights and the corresponding benchmark evaluation results for every model reported in the paper.

#### Contents

1. **`arnold-final-checkpoints.tar.gz`**

   Trained model weights. Unpacks to: `<Arnold-root>/data/final_checkpoints/`

   ~2.8 GB. One subdirectory per model (see "Models" below), each containing per-seed subdirectories (`seed_0`, `seed_1`, ...).

   A typical seed directory contains:

   * `rl_model_<steps>_steps.zip` — Stable-Baselines3 policy checkpoint
   * `rl_model_vecnormalize_<steps>_steps.pkl` — VecNormalize statistics
   * `model_config.json` / `args.json` — training + model configuration
   * `<Task>_config.json` — per-task environment configs
   * `vocabulary.json` — sensorimotor vocabulary (where used)
   * `main_bc_ppo_multi_task.py` — training entry point (snapshot)
   * `PPO_0/` — training logs / TensorBoard events

2. **`arnold-benchmark-results.tar.gz`**

   Benchmark evaluation results. Unpacks to: `<Arnold-root>/data/final_benchmarks/`

   ~4 MB. Same model/seed layout as above; each seed directory holds:

   * `seed_<n>_<checkpoint>_results.json` — per-task benchmark scores
   * `*.log` — evaluation run logs

3. **`arnold-benchmark-results-extra.tar.gz`**

   Benchmark evaluation results. Unpacks to: `<Arnold-root>/data/final_benchmarks_extra/`

   ~11 MB. Contains files used by plotting or other analysis in the paper.

4. **`expert-policies.tar.gz`**

   Expert checkpoints. Unpacks to: `<Arnold-root>/data/expert_policies/`

   ~687 MB.

5. **`kinesis.tar.gz`**

   Model files and data for the Walk-to-point (Kinesis) task. Unpacks to: `<Arnold-root>/data/kinesis/`

   ~29 MB.

| Model                        | Description                                          |

| `obc_m` / `obc_s` / `obc_xs` | OBC capacity variants (medium / small / extra-small) |
| `obc_st`                     | OBC single-task specialists                          |
| `obc_task_sv`                | OBC, task-specific sensorimotor vocabulary variant   |
| `obc_ppo`                    | OBC with PPO fine-tuning                             |
| `obc_wo_obs_norm`            | OBC ablation without observation normalization       |
| `bc`                         | Behavior-cloning baseline                            |
| `ppo_t`                      | Transformer-based PPO (no sensorimotor vocabulary)   |
| `ppo_t_sv`                   | Transformer-based PPO with sensorimotor vocabulary   |
| `mt-ppo`                     | Multi-task PPO                                       |
| `mt-sac`                     | Multi-task SAC                                       |

indexableObject.name: Pre-shot RAPTOR-FBT simulations of TCV ohmic and NBI-heated discharges

dc.description.abstract.value:
Associated publication

[1] C.E. Contré et al 2026 Nucl. Fusion 66 086053

General description

This dataset contains predictive simulations of TCV tokamak discharges performed using the RAPTOR [2] fast radial transport code. Transport fluxes are estimated with a gradient-based transport model [3], newly extended to model transitions from Positive (PT) to Negative Triangularity confinement and include ion temperature modeling [1]. Simulations were run predictively from the pulse schedule, using only the line-averaged density from experiment (model E1 in [1]).

Equilibrium is computed using FBT [4], an inverse free-boundary equilibrium code of the MEQ suite. Both RAPTOR and FBT are coded in Matlab and versioned with Git. 

The 211 shots were selected based on data availability and heating scheme (fully ohmic or with NBI) in the range 82000-82999, which corresponds to a period of approximately 2 months of TCV experiments. 

More details about the methodology used can be found in the publication of reference [1]. 

Format

indexableObject.name: Braided Rivers as Morphological States: A Data-Driven Identification of Recurrent Planform Configurations

dc.description.abstract.value:
Braided rivers undergo continuous reorganization of their channel network, producing highly dynamic planform evolution and strongly intermittent sediment transport. Despite this apparent complexity, recent research suggests that braided rivers repeatedly occupy a finite number of characteristic morphological configurations, referred to as morphological states. Identifying these recurrent configurations provides a compact framework for describing and modeling river morphodynamics.

This repository contains the complete set of binary water masks extracted from a long-duration laboratory experiment conducted at the Laboratory of Environmental Hydraulics (LHE), École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), Switzerland. The experiment consisted of a 3.3 m × 1.0 m mobile-bed flume operated under constant water discharge (0.15 L s⁻¹) and constant sediment feed rate (1.5 g s⁻¹) for approximately 1,200 hours. Overhead images of the braided river were acquired every minute and processed using an automated image-processing workflow based on HSV color segmentation to extract the wetted area of the channel as binary masks.

The masks constitute the primary dataset used in the companion studies Braided Rivers as Morphological States: A Data-Driven Identification of Recurrent Planform Configurations and Morphological State Transitions and Sediment Transport Variability in Braided Rivers. In the first study, the masks were used to identify recurrent morphological states through image similarity analysis, dimensionality reduction, and density-based clustering. In the second study, these identified states formed the basis for a stochastic description of braided-river evolution and a probabilistic model of sediment transport variability.

The dataset is intended to support research in river morphodynamics, geomorphology, sediment transport, computer vision, machine learning, and image analysis. By providing the complete sequence of binary masks, the repository enables reproducibility of the published analyses and facilitates the development and benchmarking of new methods for image-based characterization of river morphology.

indexableObject.name: CleanCloud CHOPIN - radar data & code

dc.description.abstract.value:
This repository contains the code & data referenced in the ESSD manuscript "Multi-frequency radar measurements of clouds and precipitation collected during the 2024-2025 CHOPIN campaign at Mt. Helmos".

Manuscript abstract:

This article describes the dataset of cloud and precipitation measurements collected during the CleanCloud Helmos OrograPhic sIte experimeNt (CHOPIN) campaign, conducted from October 2024 to January 2025 on Mt. Helmos, Peloponnese, Greece. The data were collected by the Environmental Remote Sensing Laboratory of the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL) and comprise coordinated observations from X- and Ka-band dual-polarisation Doppler radars and a W-band Doppler cloud profiler, complemented by 37 radiosonde profiles. Precipitation occurred for approximately 440 hours, resulting in roughly 1.2 m of snow accumulation at the remote sensing site. Two precipitation events are presented to illustrate the two main cloud and precipitation regimes captured in the dataset. The first event, between 6 and 8 January 2025, captures a succession of shallow turbulent orographic clouds interspersed with higher non-precipitating clouds, with a brief episode of surface-reaching precipitation from the upper cloud layer. The second case study, on 15 January 2025, shows a mixed-phase precipitation system dominated by primary ice nucleation near cloud top, particle growth through deposition and aggregation, and signatures of riming in the lower cloud layers, within a dynamically evolving synoptic context. Together, these examples highlight the potential of multi-frequency radar observations in an orographic winter setting for investigating cloud microphysics, particle growth processes, and aerosol--cloud interactions in mixed-phase clouds. As a dataset combining wintertime orographic conditions with coordinated multi-frequency radar observations, and collected alongside an extensive suite of in situ cloud microphysical and aerosol measurements within the broader CleanCloud campaign, the CHOPIN radar data opens new possibilities for mixed-phase cloud microphysics and aerosol-cloud interaction studies.

Note that L1 radar data (in netCDF format) is available on the ACTRIS Cloudnet data portal, instruments "LAPI MXPol weather radar", "LATMOS BASTA Doppler non-scanning cloud radar" and "METEK MIRA-35S (MBR5) Doppler scanning cloud radar" (more details can be found in the manuscript).

indexableObject.name: Momentum space imaging of ultra-thin electron liquids in δ-doped silicon

dc.description.abstract.value: Dataset: SX-ARPES raw data, processed data and the codes used for analysing and data fitting our work at doi/10.1002/advs.202302101 are all available here. The theoretical mdelling is also avaiable. Abstract: Two-dimensional dopant layers (δ-layers) in semiconductors provide the high-mobility electron liquids (2DELs) needed for nanoscale quantum-electronic devices. Key parameters such as carrier densities, effective masses, and confinement thicknesses for 2DELs have traditionally been extracted from quantum magnetotransport. In principle, the parameters are immediately readable from the one-electron spectral function that can be measured by angle-resolved photoemission (ARPES). Here, we measure buried 2DEL δ-layers in silicon with soft X-ray (SX) ARPES to obtain detailed information about their filled conduction bands and extract device-relevant properties. We take advantage of the larger probing depth and photon energy range of SX-ARPES relative to vacuum ultraviolet (VUV) ARPES to accurately measure the δ-layer electronic confinement. Our measurements are made on ambient-exposed samples and yield extremely thin (< 1 nm) and dense (~1014 cm-2) 2DELs. Critically, we use this method to show that δ-layers of arsenic exhibit better electronic confinement than δ-layers of phosphorus fabricated under identical conditions.

indexableObject.name: Practical Tools for Personal and Sensitive Research Data - Curated Table

dc.description.abstract.value:
This resource is a community-maintained curated table of practical software tools that researchers can use to manipulate personal or sensitive data throughout the research lifecycle. It was produced by members of Work Group 1 (WG1) of the Personal Data Support Network (PDSN) node, within the Swiss Research Data Support Network (SRDSN) (researchdatasupport.ch).

The table is intended to help researchers, data stewards, and support staff at Swiss higher education institutions (HEIs) identify suitable tools for handling personal or sensitive research data in a privacy-respecting and legally compliant manner.The table covers only tools that researchers actively use (or can use) to manipulate data., so it does not include guides on compliance procedures nor training material.

The table is organized into 6 thematic sheets: Collection, Transcribe, Pseudo & Anonymize, Share, Encrypt, and Others. Each tool entry is described along consistent dimensions: main function, use case, open-source status, technical complexity (Nerd Degree), data type, deployment model, AI/ML usage, Swiss institutional support, and comments.

This dataset includes the curated table in two formats (ODS and XLSX) and a README file. The information is provided on a best-effort basis; contributors do not assume responsibility for its accuracy, completeness, or currency. Users are advised to verify tool-specific information - especially regarding legal compliance and data protection - before making decisions.

### Supplementary Data — Trained Model Checkpoints and Benchmark Results

This archive set accompanies an anonymous manuscript submission. It contains the final trained model weights and the corresponding benchmark evaluation results for every model reported in the paper.

#### Contents

1. **`arnold-final-checkpoints.tar.gz`**

   Trained model weights. Unpacks to: `<Arnold-root>/data/final_checkpoints/`

   ~2.8 GB. One subdirectory per model (see "Models" below), each containing per-seed subdirectories (`seed_0`, `seed_1`, ...).

   A typical seed directory contains:

   * `rl_model_<steps>_steps.zip` — Stable-Baselines3 policy checkpoint
   * `rl_model_vecnormalize_<steps>_steps.pkl` — VecNormalize statistics
   * `model_config.json` / `args.json` — training + model configuration
   * `<Task>_config.json` — per-task environment configs
   * `vocabulary.json` — sensorimotor vocabulary (where used)
   * `main_bc_ppo_multi_task.py` — training entry point (snapshot)
   * `PPO_0/` — training logs / TensorBoard events

2. **`arnold-benchmark-results.tar.gz`**

   Benchmark evaluation results. Unpacks to: `<Arnold-root>/data/final_benchmarks/`

   ~4 MB. Same model/seed layout as above; each seed directory holds:

   * `seed_<n>_<checkpoint>_results.json` — per-task benchmark scores
   * `*.log` — evaluation run logs

3. **`arnold-benchmark-results-extra.tar.gz`**

   Benchmark evaluation results. Unpacks to: `<Arnold-root>/data/final_benchmarks_extra/`

   ~11 MB. Contains files used by plotting or other analysis in the paper.

4. **`expert-policies.tar.gz`**

   Expert checkpoints. Unpacks to: `<Arnold-root>/data/expert_policies/`

   ~687 MB.

5. **`kinesis.tar.gz`**

   Model files and data for the Walk-to-point (Kinesis) task. Unpacks to: `<Arnold-root>/data/kinesis/`

   ~29 MB.

dc.description.abstract.value:
The Atlas of Regenerative Materials

The Atlas of Regenerative Materials is collecting knowledge and know-how on availability and use of regenerative materials for construction. Data is structured in 5 entities: Resource, Buidling Material, Construction Technique, Professionals and Buildings. Taxonomies for all entities and for buiding elements help filter the dataset. 

Every entry consists at least of: - Title- Descriptive Text- Material Tag (Earth, Straw, Hemp, Wood, Stone, Other Fibres, Re-Used)- One multimedia item- Entry author

Where applicable, adress(es), relations to other entries or to taxonomy items, external links and other entity-specific details can be added, as well as further textual information.

Data on Zenodo

Here on this repository we share and store snapshots every 12 months. The dataset consists of tables for each entity of the Atlas of Regenerative Materials and the authors as well as the taxonomies. Additionnally GIS data on resource potentials is available for Switzerland and parts of Europe as far as they are being produced.

Data structure from snapshots



Entities: Here are all textual inputs and relations from the entries, grouped by entity

Files: Here lie all multimedia documents related to the entries

Taxonomies: All taxonomies used for characterisation of the entries

indexableObject.name: ArmEpiC – Armenian Epigraphic Corpus (ArtsakhEpiC Sub-Corpus).

dc.description.abstract.value:
ArmEpiC: Methodology and Data Description 

ArmEpiC, Armenian Epigraphic Corpus (ArtsakhEpiC Sub-Corpus), is a digital scholarly edition of ten Armenian lapidary inscriptions from Artsakh, diplomatically transcribed and encoded in TEI/EpiDoc (v9.7), together with the controlled-vocabulary authority files needed to interpret them. ArtsakhEpiC is the Artsakh regional sub-corpus of the wider ArmEpiC (Armenian Epigraphic Corpus) initiative, hosted by the EPFL Digital Humanities Laboratory (DHLAB).

Scope of the dataset. The deposit includes ten TEI/EpiDoc inscription files (ART0001–ART0010), each a standalone document with diplomatic transcription, translations in Armenian and English, physical description, dating, and bibliography; twelve authority files covering places and toponyms (ListPlace), monuments and monument parts (ListMonument), preservation and condition states (ListPreservation, cross-referenced to the EAGLE preservation-state vocabulary and Getty AAT), materials (ListMaterial), scripts and hands (ListScript), techniques (ListTechniques), object types (ListObjectType), inscription functional types (ListInscriptionType), abbreviation types (ListAbbreviationType), chronology and dating methods (ListChronology), bibliography (ListBibl), and editors and contributors (ListEditors); ten photographic figures (Fig. 1–Fig. 10, one per inscription); a README; and a licensing statement.

Standards and encoding. All XML files are TEI/EpiDoc 9.7, associated via <?xml-model?> processing instructions with the schema at https://epidoc.stoa.org/schema/9.7/tei-epidoc.rng (both RelaxNG structure and embedded Schematron rules). Authority files are aligned with CIDOC CRM and, where applicable, cross-referenced to EAGLE and the Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus. Each authority entity carries a persistent URN of the form urn:armepic:<vocabulary>:<ID>, and every inscription's editorial responsibility statement references the corresponding editor URN in ListEditors.

Editors and contributors. Hamest Tamrazyan (EPFL DHLAB) — editor-in-chief: project direction, template development, EpiDoc adaptation, terminology and SKOS modelling, authority-file creation. Gayane Hovhannisyan (European University of Armenia) — editor: translation of texts and terminology, EpiDoc adaptation, validation of terminology and SKOS concepts. Arsen Harutyunyan (Institute of Archaeology and Ethnography, NAS RA) — editor: epigraphic research and provision of inscriptional data, EpiDoc adaptation, photographic data collection. Emanuela Boros (EPFL DHLAB) — data curator: technical implementation support, data curation, project co-supervision. Emile Cornamusaz (EPFL) — contributor: technical implementation and automation.

Licensing and versioning. The dataset is released under a Creative Commons Attribution–NonCommercial 4.0 International (CC BY-NC 4.0) license; reuse for research and teaching is welcome with attribution, and commercial use requires the editors' permission. This Zenodo deposit represents a fixed release; future revisions will receive new versions under the same concept DOI.

Funding. This project has been funded by the National Association for Armenian Studies and Research (NAASR), the Knights of Vartan Fund for Armenian Studies, and the Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF, grants IZSEZ0_212008 and IZSEZ0_216747).

What changed in this version. This release corrects a broad set of issues found in the previously published deposit: four inscription files that were not well-formed XML; the editor authority file, rebuilt as a valid, schema-associated TEI document with persistent URNs matching those already referenced by the inscriptions; a license inconsistency across files, now unified to CC BY-NC 4.0 throughout; a missing ListPreservation authority file, now added, resolving preservation-state references used by six of the ten inscriptions; a dead schema URL in all ten inscription files, repointed to the working one already used by the authority files; and filename/asset naming inconsistencies. All 22 XML files were additionally validated against the live EpiDoc 9.7 RelaxNG schema, surfacing and fixing further schema violations across the inscription files (invalid <license> spelling, duplicate single-occurrence elements, misplaced header elements, an invalid content-model mixture in the source description, out-of-order manuscript-identifier elements, and a misplaced pointing attribute) and one authority file (a header ordering error). One inscription record, ART0009, additionally had its title and inscription-type classification corrected: it had been copy-pasted from another record and mislabeled the wrong monument (Gandzasar instead of Dadivank).

dc.description.abstract.value:
General information



Author info: Jules GRANDVILLEMIN, PhD Candidate, EPFL (https://orcid.org/0009-0009-4663-6120).

Date of collection: 19 December, 2025.


 

Description



This dataset provides all the data needed to reproduce the results of a submitted article that evaluates the potential (i.e. possibilities) to practice sustainable mobility in a given area.

To do this, the author calculated three scores, the formulas and data used for each of which are listed in the 'Methodological info' section in the README.txt file:


(i) a score for accessibility to essential daily human needs on foot or by public transport (PT);

(ii) a score for individual motility, i.e. their ability to use PT;

(iii) a synthetic score combining the two previous scores: i.e. accessibility and mobility.



Please note that, for ethical reasons, we removed the personal identifiers and residential locations of the surveyed individuals from the dataset. 

However, the results are reproducible because we:



Used the centre of 1580 x 1km² cells (where individuals' residences are located) as the origin of the travels to calculate the accessibility score, so their residence's localisation is not needed;

Transmitted all the data used to obtain the results (file data) that we spatialised through the 1 km² cells (SMP_dataset.zip/data/results.gpkg).

indexableObject.name: Data from: Tethering and depth of submergence affect the swimming performance of undulatory robots

dc.description.abstract.value:
This directory contains open-source data obtained at the UNFoLD laboratory and BioRob laboratory at EPFL. The data were recorded using the bio-inspired undulatory robot 1-guilla, swimming freely in a pool and tethered in a water channel at various depths. #### Related article The methods and results are described in the paper: *Anastasiadis. A, Ijspeert. A. J., & Mulleners, K. (2026). Tethering and depth of submergence affect the swimming performance of undulatory robots, 2026. arXiv preprint arXiv:2605.03850.* Related article abstract:
Over the past few decades, biomimetic robotic experiments have significantly advanced our understanding of undulatory swimming. Compared to animal experiments, robotic experiments offer repeatability and controlled parameter variations, but the robots operate under constraints that differ from those experienced by their natural counterparts. Freely swimming robots often remain on the surface, whereas most undulatory fish, including eels, are typically fully submerged during locomotion. Studies focusing on submerged swimming commonly rely on tethered robots to maintain depth control. This study examines the performance implications for free versus tethered swimming at the surface, and for tethered swimming at the surface to tethered fully submerged swimming, using the robotic undulatory swimmer 1-guilla. The robot was tested in two configurations: free swimming in a pool and tethered swimming in a water channel at the surface and at varying depths down to three body heights. We varied kinematic input parameters and quantified performance in terms of swimming speed, cost of transport, and body kinematics. Our results reveal that at the surface, tethered swimming achieves speeds comparable to free swimming but at a lower energetic cost. This reduction in cost of transport is attributed to the mechanical stabilisation imposed by tethering, including the suppression of body roll and lateral head motion. Increasing submergence depth improved both the maximum speed and energy efficiency by more than 10% relative to the surface swimming performance. As the body kinematics remained unchanged when submerged, the performance deficit near the surface is attributed to increased wave drag. Overall, our findings provide explanations and insights into discrepancies in results obtained for tethered and free-swimming robotic studies, they highlight the hydrodynamic challenges of surface locomotion, and can help explain why natural undulatory swimmers predominantly favour submerged propulsion.
#### Structure overview This data repository contains the following files: \- `resultsFree.csv` - Experimental parameters and calculated results for experiments with the free swimming version of 1-guilla in the pool. \- `resultsTeth.csv` - Experimental parameters and calculated results for experiments with the tethered swimming version of 1-guilla in the water channel. \- `kinematicsFree/kinematics_msXXXmptYYY_free.csv` - containing individual recorded kinematics for the free-swimming version of the robot in the pool. \- `kinematicsTeth/kinematics_msXXXmptYYY_teth.csv` - containing individual recorded kinematics for the tethered swimming version of the robot in the water. channel \- `load_data.m` - Initial support for loading and visualisation of the data is provided in this file  The data structure and variable descriptions are included in the `readme.md`.

dc.description.abstract.value:
Associated publication

[1] C.E. Contré et al 2026 Nucl. Fusion 66 086053

General description

This dataset contains predictive simulations of TCV tokamak discharges performed using the RAPTOR [2] fast radial transport code. Transport fluxes are estimated with a gradient-based transport model [3], newly extended to model transitions from Positive (PT) to Negative Triangularity confinement and include ion temperature modeling [1]. Simulations were run predictively from the pulse schedule, using only the line-averaged density from experiment (model E1 in [1]).

Equilibrium is computed using FBT [4], an inverse free-boundary equilibrium code of the MEQ suite. Both RAPTOR and FBT are coded in Matlab and versioned with Git. 

The 211 shots were selected based on data availability and heating scheme (fully ohmic or with NBI) in the range 82000-82999, which corresponds to a period of approximately 2 months of TCV experiments. 

More details about the methodology used can be found in the publication of reference [1]. 

Format

Results are sampled down to a 2ms time step and stored in the IMAS-3.0 IDS (hdf5) format [5,6] for easy share among the fusion community. This format follows the FAIR principles. Documentation can be found at: https://imas-data-dictionary.readthedocs.io/.

indexableObject.name: Braided Rivers as Morphological States: A Data-Driven Identification of Recurrent Planform Configurations

dc.description.abstract.value:
Braided rivers undergo continuous reorganization of their channel network, producing highly dynamic planform evolution and strongly intermittent sediment transport. Despite this apparent complexity, recent research suggests that braided rivers repeatedly occupy a finite number of characteristic morphological configurations, referred to as morphological states. Identifying these recurrent configurations provides a compact framework for describing and modeling river morphodynamics.

This repository contains the complete set of binary water masks extracted from a long-duration laboratory experiment conducted at the Laboratory of Environmental Hydraulics (LHE), École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), Switzerland. The experiment consisted of a 3.3 m × 1.0 m mobile-bed flume operated under constant water discharge (0.15 L s⁻¹) and constant sediment feed rate (1.5 g s⁻¹) for approximately 1,200 hours. Overhead images of the braided river were acquired every minute and processed using an automated image-processing workflow based on HSV color segmentation to extract the wetted area of the channel as binary masks.

The masks constitute the primary dataset used in the companion studies Braided Rivers as Morphological States: A Data-Driven Identification of Recurrent Planform Configurations and Morphological State Transitions and Sediment Transport Variability in Braided Rivers. In the first study, the masks were used to identify recurrent morphological states through image similarity analysis, dimensionality reduction, and density-based clustering. In the second study, these identified states formed the basis for a stochastic description of braided-river evolution and a probabilistic model of sediment transport variability.

The dataset is intended to support research in river morphodynamics, geomorphology, sediment transport, computer vision, machine learning, and image analysis. By providing the complete sequence of binary masks, the repository enables reproducibility of the published analyses and facilitates the development and benchmarking of new methods for image-based characterization of river morphology.

indexableObject.name: CleanCloud CHOPIN - radar data & code

dc.description.abstract.value:
This repository contains the code & data referenced in the ESSD manuscript "Multi-frequency radar measurements of clouds and precipitation collected during the 2024-2025 CHOPIN campaign at Mt. Helmos".

Manuscript abstract:

This article describes the dataset of cloud and precipitation measurements collected during the CleanCloud Helmos OrograPhic sIte experimeNt (CHOPIN) campaign, conducted from October 2024 to January 2025 on Mt. Helmos, Peloponnese, Greece. The data were collected by the Environmental Remote Sensing Laboratory of the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL) and comprise coordinated observations from X- and Ka-band dual-polarisation Doppler radars and a W-band Doppler cloud profiler, complemented by 37 radiosonde profiles. Precipitation occurred for approximately 440 hours, resulting in roughly 1.2 m of snow accumulation at the remote sensing site. Two precipitation events are presented to illustrate the two main cloud and precipitation regimes captured in the dataset. The first event, between 6 and 8 January 2025, captures a succession of shallow turbulent orographic clouds interspersed with higher non-precipitating clouds, with a brief episode of surface-reaching precipitation from the upper cloud layer. The second case study, on 15 January 2025, shows a mixed-phase precipitation system dominated by primary ice nucleation near cloud top, particle growth through deposition and aggregation, and signatures of riming in the lower cloud layers, within a dynamically evolving synoptic context. Together, these examples highlight the potential of multi-frequency radar observations in an orographic winter setting for investigating cloud microphysics, particle growth processes, and aerosol--cloud interactions in mixed-phase clouds. As a dataset combining wintertime orographic conditions with coordinated multi-frequency radar observations, and collected alongside an extensive suite of in situ cloud microphysical and aerosol measurements within the broader CleanCloud campaign, the CHOPIN radar data opens new possibilities for mixed-phase cloud microphysics and aerosol-cloud interaction studies.

Note that L1 radar data (in netCDF format) is available on the ACTRIS Cloudnet data portal, instruments "LAPI MXPol weather radar", "LATMOS BASTA Doppler non-scanning cloud radar" and "METEK MIRA-35S (MBR5) Doppler scanning cloud radar" (more details can be found in the manuscript).

indexableObject.name: Practical Tools for Personal and Sensitive Research Data - Curated Table

dc.description.abstract.value:
This resource is a community-maintained curated table of practical software tools that researchers can use to manipulate personal or sensitive data throughout the research lifecycle. It was produced by members of Work Group 1 (WG1) of the Personal Data Support Network (PDSN) node, within the Swiss Research Data Support Network (SRDSN) (researchdatasupport.ch).

The table is intended to help researchers, data stewards, and support staff at Swiss higher education institutions (HEIs) identify suitable tools for handling personal or sensitive research data in a privacy-respecting and legally compliant manner.The table covers only tools that researchers actively use (or can use) to manipulate data., so it does not include guides on compliance procedures nor training material.

The table is organized into 6 thematic sheets: Collection, Transcribe, Pseudo & Anonymize, Share, Encrypt, and Others. Each tool entry is described along consistent dimensions: main function, use case, open-source status, technical complexity (Nerd Degree), data type, deployment model, AI/ML usage, Swiss institutional support, and comments.

This dataset includes the curated table in two formats (ODS and XLSX) and a README file. The information is provided on a best-effort basis; contributors do not assume responsibility for its accuracy, completeness, or currency. Users are advised to verify tool-specific information - especially regarding legal compliance and data protection - before making decisions.

*Contact author:* damien.gilliard@epfl.ch, or via an issue on the github repository

#### Content

Thank you for your interest in diffCheck 2! This zenodo dataset contains the data and code needed to reproduce the results presented in the paper called "Design-Integrated Scan-to-CAD Evaluation for Incremental Fabrication Workflows", presented at DMS 2026. The code used is the version 2.0.0 of the [github repository](https://github.com/diffCheckOrg/diffCheck)

As diffCheck relies on algorithms such as RanSaC and K-means clustering, exact reproduction is impossible to garantee. When possible, transformation used were saved and can be re-applied to the data. We also provide the CSV files used in the paper.

#### Repoduction steps.

For both experiment we provide a README containing the main reproduction steps.

indexableObject.name: Dataset: Modelling human activities in a system of cities

dc.description.abstract.value: This repository contains the input data for the paper 'Modelling human activities in a system of cities'.  The input data is used to run the DAVE model for Cantons Vaud and Geneva in Switzerland at 500m grid. DAVE (**D**ynamic **A**nthropogenic acti**V**ities and feedback to **E**missions) is a multi-scale agent-based modelling system. It uses a bottom-up approach to model the interactions and feedback between urban form (e.g., building morphology, materials), urban function determined by human activities and the urban micro-climate. This dataset is organized following the structure required by DAVE. Further details can be found at:  - DAVE Documentation and Manual:  [10.5281/zenodo.11369892](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.11369893) The top folders containing the files for each category: Citizens, EnvironmentalVariables, InputOptions, Spatial, Time_settings, Transport, Travel_dict. **Citizens:** each citizen in each grid with household and building information **EnvironmentalVariables:** weather forcing **InputOptions:** microenvironments and age type definitions Spatial: - Information on the spatial grids such as the grid list, employment rate, spatial attractor, commuting attractor.  - Information on building such as the initial occupancy of each building (London_stebbs_building_typologies.nml actually contains building in the Swiss domain) and general thermal properties (London_stebbs_general_params.nml, currently uses London parameters but can be updated in the future)  **Time_settings:** day types (weekday, holidays, holidays with school) of each day of year **Transport:** transport capacity of each mode. The probability of using each transport mode to commute at each grid.  **Travel_dict:** the shortest path for each transport mode between each 500m grid in the study domain. The files are produced by MATSDA (**M**ovement **A**nd **T**ransport **S**imulations using **D**ijkstra’s **A**lgorithm) v1.0, which uses grid-based transport database and Dijkstra’s Algorithm to solve the shortest paths between each grid. Further details can be found at: - Connecting Physical and Socio-Economic Spaces for Multi-Scale Urban Modelling: A Dataset for London. Geoscience Data Journal 12: e289. https://doi.org/10.1002/gdj3.289  - The transport network input to MATSDA can be downloaded from SwissTopo: https://www.swisstopo.admin.ch/en/landscape-model-swisstlm3d - Note: a newer version of MATSDA has become available recently (not used in this study): MATSDA-roads (Movement And Transport Simulations using Dijkstra's Algorithm - roads), https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17736682 To run DAVE simulations, a file on population activity schedule/habits is also needed. We processed this file from the TimeUse+ survey conducted by ETHZ but is not able to share it due to privacy. The data from TimeUse+ survey can be requested from its authors. Further details can be found at:  -  TimeUse+ main study Anonymized data, http://hdl.handle.net/20.500.11850/639241 More details on the processes to produce these files can be found at:  - Connecting Physical and Socio-Economic Spaces for Multi-Scale Urban Modelling: A Dataset for London. indexableObject.name: DATASET for "Validity of Independent Control in the [Blob-Detection-Based Photonic] Design Framework"

dc.description.abstract.value:
This dataset contains numerically generated correlated disordered patterns for metasurfaces and their simulated optical scattering responses. The structures consist of cylindrical or ring-shaped dielectric scatterers with a constant refractive index n = 3.5 and height h = 200 nm on a substrate of the same material. The dataset explores how the optical scattering response changes as the spatial-frequency content is controlled in single and superimposed metasurfaces.

The dataset is organized around comparing the collective scattering response of the metasurface to the forward-scattering efficiency, Qscat, of a single nanoresonator.The term "CLR vs Qscat" is used throughout the dataset as a naming convention for this comparison. It does not correspond to a directly stored variable in the data files. The raw simulation outputs contain wavelength-resolved power quantities (e.g., source power, transmitted power, and far-field power).

The analysis and visualization of the collective response (CLR) are performed through post-processing using the provided Jupyter notebooks and Python functions.

Qscat is provided separately as a reference dataset for isolated scatterers.

Methodology for pattern generation and calculation can be found in the associated thesis.

indexableObject.name: DATASET for Multi-Resonant Correlated-Disordered Metasurfaces for Light Trapping

dc.description.abstract.value:
This dataset contains pattern designs and related simulation data for studying light trapping in nanostructured zinc phosphide (Zn₃P₂) thin films. 

The dataset includes:

* Optical constants for Ag and Zn₃P₂ used in simulations
* Guided mode resonance calculations for Zn₃P₂ slabs
* Forward scattering cross sections for individual nanostructures
* Light-trapping patterns (multi-resonant periodic, correlated-disordered and multi-resonant correlated-disordered designs), provided as images, coordinate files, and GDS layouts
* Absorption spectra from FDTD simulations of patterned Zn₃P₂ films on Ag substrates

Full methodological details are available in the associated PhD thesis.
